articles.title: The Bakery That Never Asked
articles.dek: A New York bakery built its business on a list anyone could sign. Nineteen centuries earlier, a letter to tired Christians asked them to feel the chains of the people everyone else had decided to forget.
articles.quote: To remember a prisoner, in the Bible's sense, is to feel the chain on your own wrist and then go and knock on the door.
articles.body:
Near the front door of a bakery in Yonkers, New York, there is a list, and anyone may sign it. Nobody hands you an application form or asks for a résumé, and there is no box asking whether you have ever been convicted of a crime. You write your name and a phone number, and when a job opens on the production floor, the bakery calls the next name on the list. For a man who has spent years behind bars, and then long months hearing employers promise to "keep his file on record," that sheet of paper can feel like the first open door he has seen since the prison gates closed behind him.

The bakery is Greyston, founded in 1982 by Bernie Glassman, a former aerospace engineer who wanted to build a business in a neighborhood many companies had abandoned. He called the practice "open hiring," and the company was built around a sentence that has since been repeated in business schools around the world: "We don't hire people to bake brownies. We bake brownies to hire people." The brownies are real, and very good. For decades Greyston has supplied the fudgy chunks folded into Ben & Jerry's ice cream. The harder problem Glassman set out to solve, however, was what to do about people whom the rest of society had quietly agreed to forget.

The idea carried real risk, and managers worried openly about theft and turnover. Over the years the company found that many people who were finally given a chance treated it as something precious, and with steady training and support, a list of strangers became a skilled workforce. Greyston was honest about where people had come from. It simply decided that a person's past would be the starting point of the conversation and never the end of it.

Nearly two thousand years earlier, a pastor wrote to a church that understood exactly what it meant to be forgotten. We do not know his name, but his letter, which we call Hebrews, was written to Jewish believers in Jesus who had grown weary and were tempted to drift back into the safer religion of their childhood. Earlier in their story they had been remarkably brave. The writer reminds them of those days: "You suffered along with those in prison and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property" (Hebrews 10:34). Years had passed since then, and the courage was wearing thin. After twelve chapters of soaring argument about Jesus as the great High Priest, the writer brings everything down to the ground in chapter 13 with a series of plain, practical instructions. The first is "Keep on loving one another as brothers and sisters" (Hebrews 13:1), the second is to welcome strangers, and the third concerns the people in chains.

To feel the weight of that third instruction, picture a prison in the first-century Roman world. It was mostly a holding place, a dark room where the accused waited, sometimes for months, for a trial or a sentence. The state rarely fed the prisoners well, if at all. Bread, water, a blanket, and a little lamp oil came from family and friends who were willing to show up at the door, and showing up was dangerous. Every visit announced to the guards and the neighbors that you belonged to this person and shared whatever shame was attached to his name.

The apostle Paul knew that loneliness from the inside. Chained in Rome near the end of his life, he wrote that many of his companions had turned away from him. Then he remembered one man with deep gratitude. A believer named Onesiphorus had traveled to the capital and, in Paul's words, "he searched hard for me until he found me" (2 Timothy 1:17). You can almost see him walking from one guardhouse to the next, asking soldiers where the Jewish prisoner from Tarsus was being held, knowing that every question marked him as a friend of a condemned man. Paul's verdict on him is beautiful: "he often refreshed me and was not ashamed of my chains" (2 Timothy 1:16). That is the kind of love the writer of Hebrews is asking his tired church to recover.

"Continue to remember those in prison as if you were together with them in prison, and those who are mistreated as if you yourselves were suffering." (Hebrews 13:3)

The phrase "together with them in prison" translates a single Greek word, syndedemenoi, which means "bound together with." It comes from the same root as the word for a chain. The writer is asking his readers to imagine the iron on their own wrists, to feel the cold floor and the hunger of the night as though they were sitting beside the prisoner in the dark. The second half of the verse goes further still. Read literally, the Greek says to remember the mistreated "since you yourselves are also in the body." One way to read this is as a reminder of shared fragility. You have skin that bruises and a stomach that aches when it is empty, and the same body that lets you feel your own pain is the doorway through which you can feel someone else's.

The word "remember" carries weight as well. In Scripture, remembering is something God does with his hands. When the flood covered the earth, "God remembered Noah and all the wild animals and the livestock that were with him in the ark, and he sent a wind over the earth, and the waters receded" (Genesis 8:1). God's remembering moved the weather. The verb in Hebrews 13:3 is also in a continuing tense, so the sense is "keep on remembering," which suggests a habit that shapes the calendar and the grocery bag. To remember a prisoner, in the Bible's sense, is to feel the chain on your own wrist and then go and knock on the door.

A few verses later, the writer tells us why this matters so much. "Jesus also suffered outside the city gate to make the people holy through his own blood. Let us, then, go to him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace he bore" (Hebrews 13:12–13). Jesus died as a condemned criminal, executed beyond the walls where respectable people would not have to look at him. When we walk toward the people the world has pushed outside, we discover that Jesus is already there. He said as much himself: "I was in prison and you came to visit me" (Matthew 25:36).

Many Filipino families carry a quiet secret about a cousin or a son who was nakulong, and the gossip in the barangay can follow that person for the rest of his life. Others have a sister working abroad who has been detained, or a kababayan who was mistreated by an employer and has no one to speak for her. Hebrews asks us to treat these people as our own flesh. In practice, that might mean bringing a packed meal on visiting day at the jail, writing a letter to someone who has not received one in months, or putting in a good word for a neighbor with a record who is trying to find honest work. It may simply mean greeting him by name after the Sunday service, warmly and in front of everyone.

The writer closes this section with a promise that holds the whole chapter together: God has said, "Never will I leave you; never will I forsake you" (Hebrews 13:5). The God who has never once forgotten you is the one who sends you toward the people others have forgotten. This week, think of one person who is behind bars or being mistreated, and let your love for that person become as practical as a name on a bakery list and a phone that finally rings.

articles.title: Barely Half the Points
articles.dek: Roger Federer won almost 80 percent of his matches but only 54 percent of his points. Ezekiel 20 tells Israel's story the same way, and one small phrase decides how it ends.
articles.quote: The final word over your record belongs to God's name, and his name has kept every promise it has ever made.
articles.body:
In June 2024, Roger Federer stood in a green academic gown before the graduating class of Dartmouth College in New Hampshire and gave a speech that traveled around the world. He had won twenty Grand Slam titles and spent years ranked first in the world, so the graduates may have expected a victory lap. He gave them a statistic instead. In 1,526 singles matches across his career, he told them, he won almost 80 percent. Then he asked what percentage of the points he had won in those matches. The answer was 54 percent.

The crowd needed a moment to take that in. One of the greatest players who ever lived lost nearly every second point he played. "When you lose every second point, on average," Federer said, "you learn not to dwell on every shot." Filipinos who have stayed up late watching Alex Eala fight through a third set understand what he meant. Look closely at any champion's record and you will find it crowded with missed returns and double faults, and yet something kept carrying that player forward into the next point and the next match.

Ezekiel 20 examines a record up close, point by point, and the score is grim. Running through the chapter, though, is a small phrase that settles the outcome, and it may be one of the most comforting phrases in the Old Testament.

Ezekiel was a young priest carried off to Babylon in 597 BC along with King Jehoiachin and thousands of Jerusalem's leading families. He lived among the exiles beside the Kebar River, far from the temple he had trained all his life to serve. The chapter just before ours is a funeral song, what Hebrew calls a qinah, a lament. In it Judah's kings are pictured as young lions caught in nets and dragged off with hooks, and as a vine that was once "fruitful and full of branches" (Ezek 19:10) before it was uprooted, thrown to the ground and replanted in a dry desert. The chapter closes with a line full of grief: "This is a lament and is to be used as a lament" (Ezek 19:14).

Then, "in the seventh year, in the fifth month on the tenth day" (Ezek 20:1), which is around August of 591 BC, some elders of Israel came and sat down in front of Ezekiel to ask a word from the LORD. We are not told their question, but exiles usually ask the same one: when can we go home? God's reply is startling. "As surely as I live, I will not let you inquire of me" (Ezek 20:3). He tells Ezekiel to walk them through their own family history instead.

The history is painful to hear. In Egypt, God swore "with uplifted hand" (Ezek 20:5) to bring them out and told them to throw away the idols they had grown fond of, "but they rebelled against me and would not listen to me" (Ezek 20:8). In the wilderness he gave them good laws and the gift of the Sabbath, "yet the people of Israel rebelled against me in the wilderness" (Ezek 20:13). He pleaded with their children to live differently from their parents, and "the children rebelled against me" (Ezek 20:21). Once settled in the land, they offered sacrifices on "any high hill or any leafy tree" (Ezek 20:28). Generation after generation, the record shows another point lost.

After each rebellion the reader braces for the end, because each time God says he was ready to pour out his wrath. Each time, the story turns on the same phrase:

"But for the sake of my name, I brought them out of Egypt. I did it to keep my name from being profaned in the eyes of the nations among whom they lived and in whose sight I had revealed myself to the Israelites by bringing them out of Egypt." (Ezekiel 20:9)

The Hebrew is lema'an shemi, "for the sake of my name," and it returns in verse 14, again in verse 22, and once more in the chapter's closing sentence. In the ancient world a name carried a person's reputation and character, the whole truth of who they were. When God revealed his name to Moses, he spelled out what it contained: "The LORD, the LORD, the compassionate and gracious God, slow to anger, abounding in love and faithfulness" (Exod 34:6). So when God says he acted for his name's sake, he is saying he acted according to who he had already declared himself to be. Israel's rescue rested on God's character, which sat beyond the reach of Israel's performance.

This also explains why God answered a question about the future with a lesson from the past. The elders wanted a date for going home. God gave them the one thing that could make any future secure, which was the proof, written across their own history, that his faithfulness had outlasted every one of their failures. The chapter ends with exactly that promise: "You will know that I am the LORD, when I deal with you for my name's sake and not according to your evil ways and your corrupt practices" (Ezek 20:44).

There is a tender, almost stubborn love in the middle of the chapter as well. The exiles were tempted to give up on God altogether and blend in with Babylon. "You say, 'We want to be like the nations,'" God reports, and then he answers, "what you have in mind will never happen" (Ezek 20:32). He promises to make them "pass under my rod" (Ezek 20:37), the image of a shepherd counting sheep one at a time as they pass under his staff (Lev 27:32). Even their plan to walk away runs into a Father who will not let them go uncounted. The rest of Scripture keeps this music going. David sings that God "guides me along the right paths for his name's sake" (Ps 23:3), and Paul writes, "if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot disown himself" (2 Tim 2:13).

This brings real peace to anyone who knows their own record. Most of us can recite our lost points better than anyone else could. Ezekiel 20 gives you permission to look at that list honestly, because God himself is the one reading it aloud, and still he keeps saying "but." Your hope for tomorrow can rest on the same ground the exiles were given, which is the steady character of the God who chose you, with your percentage set to one side.

The chapter also offers wisdom for the way we love other people. Filipino families often talk about the family name as a weight on the children: huwag mong ipahiya ang pamilya, do not bring shame on the family. In Ezekiel 20 the Father is the one who carries the name toward his children, and he lets his own reputation set the course of his love. Perhaps there is a son who has drifted, a sibling who keeps borrowing and never repays, or a spouse whose old habit has worn your patience thin. God's way allows you to tell the truth plainly, as he did with the elders, and still let your faithfulness be set by the promises you made and the person you have chosen to be. Today you might think of one person whose record you have been quietly keeping and decide what your own "but" will be, whether that is a phone call, a shared meal, or a single sentence that says you are still here.

Federer told the graduates that you lose a point and then you play the next one. The exiles by the Kebar River were given something deeper. The final word over your record belongs to God's name, and his name has kept every promise it has ever made. Whatever points you lost yesterday, you can walk into today counted, held and still his.

articles.title: The Small Hole in the Shutter
articles.dek: A thousand years ago, a scholar in a darkened room worked out how light lets us see. An ancient psalm had already described the same thing happening in the human heart.
articles.quote: Understanding begins the moment you leave the shutter open, even a crack, and let God's word come in.
articles.body:
About a thousand years ago in Cairo, a scholar named Ibn al-Haytham sat in a darkened room and watched the world appear on his wall. According to the usual story, he had promised the Caliph he could control the floods of the Nile. Standing at the river's edge, he saw that the plan could never work, and because he feared the ruler's temper, he spent years shut inside his house. Historians still debate how much of that account is true, but they agree on what he did with those years. He studied light. In a room with every window shuttered, he let daylight in through one small hole, and on the far wall appeared a living picture of the street outside, with people walking and trees moving, upside down and in full color.

That simple setup, which we now call the camera obscura, helped him settle one of the oldest arguments in science. Many great thinkers before him, including Euclid and Ptolemy, had taught that the eye sends out rays that reach toward objects, like fingers touching what they see. Through careful observation, Ibn al-Haytham showed that light travels from objects into the eye, so that seeing starts with receiving. His Book of Optics, finished around 1021, shaped how Europe would later understand vision and lenses, and eventually the camera in your phone. Every photo you have ever taken of a lola's birthday or a child's first steps rests on what he worked out in that dim room: understanding needs an opening, and light that comes in from outside.

An unnamed psalmist arrived at the same truth about God many centuries earlier. Psalm 119 is the longest chapter in the Bible, a carefully built poem of twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and every line in a stanza begins with that stanza's letter. Today's passage is the seventeenth stanza, written for the letter pe. The man writing it is under real pressure. He asks God to "redeem me from human oppression" (Psalm 119:134), and the stanza ends with him in tears: "Streams of tears flow from my eyes, for your law is not obeyed" (Psalm 119:136). He lives among people who have little use for God, and yet his first word is wonder: "Your statutes are wonderful; therefore I obey them" (Psalm 119:129). Then he writes the line that sits at the center of the stanza.

"The unfolding of your words gives light; it gives understanding to the simple." (Psalm 119:130)

The word translated "unfolding" is the Hebrew petach, and in everyday speech it meant a doorway or opening, like the spot where a tent flap is pulled back. Older translations render it "the entrance of your words." The picture is very close to Ibn al-Haytham's room. The light is already shining outside, and once an opening is made, it pours in and fills the space with an image of what is real. Even the stanza's letter fits, because pe is also the Hebrew word for "mouth," and the very next verse says, "I open my mouth and pant, longing for your commands" (Psalm 119:131). Everything in these lines leans toward openness: an open door, an open mouth, and a heart ready to receive.

The second half of the verse holds a gentle surprise. The word for "simple" is peti, which comes from a root meaning to be open. In Proverbs the word usually describes someone naive, easily led, and still unformed. Here the psalmist turns it into good news, because the person whose mind is still open, who knows how much they do not know, is exactly the one God's word lights up. One way to read the wordplay is that the opening of God's words gives light to those who are open. Jesus prayed something very close to this: "I praise you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and learned, and revealed them to little children" (Matthew 11:25).

This may be one of the kindest promises in the Psalms for anyone who has ever felt out of their depth with the Bible. Maybe you never finished school, or you finished long ago and feel your mind has grown tired. Maybe you sit in Bible study while others quote verses easily, and you quietly wonder whether Scripture was written for people smarter than you. The psalmist's answer is that the light comes from God's side of the wall. Your part is the small hole in the shutter, the willingness to let it in. Ibn al-Haytham found that a small opening actually gives the sharpest picture, and in the same way, a few verses read slowly, with a heart that says, "Lord, I want to understand," are enough for God to begin painting the truth inside you.

The stanza also shows what this light does once it gets in. The psalmist prays, "Direct my footsteps according to your word; let no sin rule over me" (Psalm 119:133), so the light that fills the mind becomes light for the feet. Then he asks for something more personal still: "Make your face shine on your servant and teach me your decrees" (Psalm 119:135). Those words echo the ancient blessing the priests spoke over Israel: "the LORD make his face shine on you and be gracious to you" (Numbers 6:25). For the psalmist, learning God's word and seeing God's smile belong together, and the light coming through the opening carries the warmth of a Person.

The apostle Paul follows this thread to its fullest point. "For God, who said, 'Let light shine out of darkness,' made his light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of God's glory displayed in the face of Christ" (2 Corinthians 4:6). The face the psalmist longed to see shining on him has a name. When you open the Gospels and read about Jesus touching a leper or welcoming a child onto his lap, the light of God's face is coming into your room.

Even the psalmist's tears belong in this picture. Verse 136 can sound severe at first, but it is the grief of someone who has seen how beautiful God's ways are and aches because others will not let the light in. Many Filipino parents know that ache well as they pray for a son working abroad who has drifted from faith, or a daughter who no longer goes to Mass or Sunday service. The psalmist shows us what to do with that sorrow. He brings it to God in the same stanza where he asks for light for himself, trusting that the God who opened his own eyes can open theirs too.

Ibn al-Haytham also learned that the image on the wall lasts only as long as the opening stays clear. If you cover the hole, the picture disappears at once. Our hearts work much the same way. Many of us start the day by opening our phones, and the first light into the room is news, messages, and worry. Tomorrow, before you unlock the screen, you might open your Bible to a single stanza of Psalm 119, just eight verses, and read it slowly while your coffee or salabat cools. Then pray the psalmist's own words, "Make your face shine on your servant" (Psalm 119:135), and ask God to show you one thing he wants you to see that day.

You do not need to be clever for this to work, because God has promised understanding to the simple, to the open, and to anyone willing to let him in. Understanding begins the moment you leave the shutter open, even a crack, and let God's word come in. The light is already shining on your side of the wall, and it is waiting for the smallest opening to show you how good and beautiful he is.

articles.title: The Man Between the Bar and the Phone
articles.dek: Proverbs paints a drinker who cannot feel his own bruises and wakes up only to go looking again. Hidden in the Hebrew is a clue that his searching was meant for something better.
articles.quote: The longing that keeps sending us back to the cup was made for God, and he is the only One who can fill it without leaving us thirstier than before.
articles.illustration: Bill Wilson's Akron hotel phone call
articles.body:
In May 1935, a New York stockbroker named Bill Wilson paced the lobby of the Mayflower Hotel in Akron, Ohio, with only about ten dollars in his pocket. He had come to Ohio for a business deal that was supposed to restore his reputation, and the deal had just fallen apart. He had been sober for roughly five months, his longest stretch in years, but he was alone in a strange city, far from his wife, and from the hotel bar came the sound of laughter and clinking glasses. Anyone who has worked far from home, eaten supper alone in a rented room, and felt the pull of whatever promises to make the night pass faster knows the weight of that moment.

On one side of the lobby was the bar. On the wall across from it hung a directory of local churches. Wilson later wrote that he realized he needed another alcoholic to talk to much more than he needed a drink. He stepped into the phone booth, dialed a minister from the board, and after a chain of calls was put in touch with a woman named Henrietta Seiberling, who knew a respected surgeon in town who was quietly drinking himself to ruin. Dr. Robert Smith agreed to give the stranger fifteen minutes on Mother's Day, and the two men ended up talking for hours. On June 10, 1935, Dr. Bob took his last drink, and the fellowship that became Alcoholics Anonymous marks that day as its beginning. Millions of people around the world, including men and women who meet in small groups across the Philippines, trace their recovery back to a lonely man who turned away from the bar and picked up a phone.

That scene is a good doorway into one of the most vivid portraits in the whole Bible. Proverbs 23 sits inside a section the book itself calls "the sayings of the wise" (Proverbs 22:17), a collection of counsel written in the voice of a father teaching his son how to live. Just before our passage, the father makes his tenderest appeal: "My son, give me your heart and let your eyes delight in my ways" (Proverbs 23:26). Then, having warned his son about one kind of seduction, he turns to another, and he does it with a riddle, the kind an older man might pose across the table after a meal.

"Who has woe? Who has sorrow? Who has strife? Who has complaints? Who has needless bruises? Who has bloodshot eyes?" (Proverbs 23:29). The word translated "sorrow" is the Hebrew 'aboy, a groan of misery that appears nowhere else in the Old Testament, as if the writer had to reach for a sound instead of a word. The answer comes at once: "Those who linger over wine, who go to sample bowls of mixed wine" (Proverbs 23:30). The father then speaks plainly to his son: "Do not gaze at wine when it is red, when it sparkles in the cup, when it goes down smoothly! In the end it bites like a snake and poisons like a viper" (Proverbs 23:31–32). The son's eyes, which the father hoped would delight in wisdom, are now fixed on the shimmer in a cup.

What follows reads almost like a comedy until you realize it is a tragedy. The drinker sees strange sights and his mind spins out confusing things (Proverbs 23:33). He is "like one sleeping on the high seas, lying on top of the rigging" (Proverbs 23:34). Israel was mostly a people of hills and farms, and to them the picture of a man dozing at the top of a ship's mast, swaying over open water and unaware of the drop below him, would have sounded like madness. Then the father lets the drinker speak for himself, and his words are the saddest in the passage.

"They hit me," you will say, "but I'm not hurt! They beat me, but I don't feel it! When will I wake up so I can find another drink?" (Proverbs 23:35)

The first half of that verse describes a man who has lost the ability to feel what is happening to him. Pain is one of God's quiet mercies, because it tells us something is wrong while there is still time to act. This man is being beaten, and the very thing that is harming him has also numbed him to the harm. His first thought on waking is a plan to go back.

The Hebrew carries a clue that is easy to miss in English. In verse 30, the word translated "sample" is chaqar, which means to search out or examine carefully. It is the same word Proverbs uses for the noble work of investigation: "It is the glory of God to conceal a matter; to search out a matter is the glory of kings" (Proverbs 25:2). In verse 35, "find another drink" is more literally "I will seek it yet again," using baqash, the very verb the father used earlier when he urged his son to pursue wisdom: "if you look for it as for silver and search for it as for hidden treasure" (Proverbs 2:4). One way to read this is that the drinker is a seeker. He has the same hunger God placed in every human heart, the hunger to search and find and be satisfied, but it has been aimed at a cup that can never hold enough.

That is why the gospel speaks to this passage with such hope. God does not ask us to stop being thirsty. He offers himself as the answer to the thirst. On the last day of a great festival, Jesus stood and called out, "Let anyone who is thirsty come to me and drink" (John 7:37). The prophet Isaiah asked the same question every addicted heart eventually asks: "Why spend money on what is not bread, and your labor on what does not satisfy?" (Isaiah 55:2). The longing that keeps sending us back to the cup was made for God, and he is the only One who can fill it without leaving us thirstier than before.

Paul brings the two halves of our proverb together in a single passage. The drinker in Proverbs asks, "When will I wake up?" Paul writes, "Wake up, sleeper, rise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you" (Ephesians 5:14), and only four verses later he adds, "Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to debauchery. Instead, be filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18). The waking the drunkard longed for is real, and it comes from Christ. When grace begins to work, feeling often returns before freedom does, and it can hurt to finally notice the bruises we ignored. That ache is a sign of life, the beginning of a heart of flesh where there had been stone (Ezekiel 36:26).

Many Filipino families know this passage from the inside. Some of us grew up with a father or uncle whose evenings of tagay slowly turned into a way of life, and some of us carry the same pull ourselves. Others will find that their own cup holds something different, such as endless scrolling at two in the morning, online betting, or work that lets us avoid feeling anything at home. The pattern is the same whenever we keep reaching for what numbs us and then wake up planning to reach again.

Bill Wilson's discovery in that hotel lobby is a very practical gift for anyone caught in that pattern. When the pull came, he moved toward a person, and that phone call became a door God opened. If something has been numbing you, the most faithful step you can take this week may be to name it out loud to one trusted believer, a pastor, or a recovery group, and to ask for help before the next evening comes. If you love someone who is still lying on top of the rigging, keep praying for their waking, keep your love steady, and do not carry the burden alone.

Whatever you are thirsty for today, that thirst is evidence that you were made for more. When you feel yourself reaching for the old cup, you can turn the moment into a prayer: "Lord, I am thirsty, and you told me to come to you." Jesus has never turned away anyone who came to him thirsty, and he will meet you there.
